title: Forty days
hookLine: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, Jesus in the desert

cards: A man alone on a mountain, with no bread and no water, while a cloud rests on the peak.

Another, worn out and wanting to die, asleep under a juniper tree in the desert until someone wakes him and puts food beside his head. A third, just baptized, walking into the wilderness with nothing.
Three stories from different parts of the Bible, and the same span of time turns up in all three. Not a week. Not a year.
Long enough to hurt, and long enough to change you. Today, forty days.

teach.h: MOSES: FORTY DAYS ON THE MOUNTAIN.
teach.b: Start with Moses. In Exodus he goes up to meet God and stays.

teach.h: ELIJAH: FORTY DAYS ON ONE MEAL.
teach.b: The King James Bible says: "And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water." He comes down carrying the words of the covenant on stone. Then Elijah.
He has run for his life and lain down to die, and an angel brings him bread and water, twice.

teach.h: JESUS: FORTY DAYS IN THE DESERT.
teach.b: "And he arose, and did eat and drink, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God."
On that mountain he hears God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. And then Jesus.

teach.h: EACH FORTY HAS A FAR SIDE.
teach.b: Matthew says: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." The tempter comes, and Jesus answers him with words from scripture. Set the three side by side.
Each is hard: hunger, exhaustion, testing. Each is spent close to God, away from the usual noise. And each one ends.
Moses comes down. Elijah arrives. Jesus walks out to begin his work.
The forty is not a life sentence; it's a passage with a far side.
That's why churches link Lent to these stories, above all to Jesus in the desert: a season long enough for something to shift, and short enough to see the end of.

This week ran from the waters of Theophany through prayer for unity, Brigid's rushes and Simeon's candle, to pancakes and a line of people saying forgive me. The last two stand at the very door of the forty days.

how: During Lent, Christians often take on a practice for the season, such as fasting, giving something up, extra prayer, or giving to the poor, and churches connect the season to Jesus's forty days in the wilderness.

o: exactly six weeks of rest before a feast

"and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb."
in each story, the forty days go on and never end
each forty ends: Moses comes down, Elijah arrives, Jesus begins his work.
Elijah heard God in the earthquake and the fire

games.q: you're Elijah, worn out under a juniper tree in the desert, ready to give up. an angel wakes you and there's bread and water by your head. what do you do?
o: eat, drink, and get up to walk.
turn over and go back to sleep for good.
games.why: he ate and drank, twice, and "went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God."

practice: Let a few ideas come for one small thing you could keep for forty days: a walk each morning, a psalm a day, or giving up something that takes too much room. Pick one, not just the first, and picture day forty.
If you pray, offer the forty days to God; if not, just hold the choice.

wordCard.voice: Forty days. The span of Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, and Jesus in the desert. A hard passage, close to God, that comes to an end.

carryVoice: Your line: forty is enough. Every forty has a far side. Rest well.
